'''Notakto''' is a [[tic-tac-toe variants|tic-tac-toe variant]], also known as '''neutral''' or '''impartial tic-tac-toe'''.<ref name=":4">{{Cite web|url=http://headinside.blogspot.com/2012/04/secrets-of-nim-notakto.html|title=Secrets of Nim (Notakto)|last=Cram|first=Scott|access-date=2016-11-25}}</ref><ref name=":2" /> The game is a combination of the games [[tic-tac-toe]] and [[Nim]],<ref name=":4" /><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://headinside.blogspot.com/2012/09/free-ios-nim-games.html|title=FREE iOS Nim Games|last=Cram|first=Scott|access-date=2016-11-25}}</ref> played across one or several boards with both of the players playing the same piece (an "X" or cross). The game ends when all the boards contain a three-in-a-row of Xs,<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://boardgamegeek.com/boardgame/204185/notakto|title=Notakto {{!}} Board Game {{!}} BoardGameGeek|website=boardgamegeek.com|access-date=2016-11-24}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://thewessens.net/ClassroomApps/Main/notakto.html?topic=probability&id=8|title=Notakto|website=thewessens.net|access-date=2016-11-24}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://markhuckvale.com/games/notakto/|title=Free Notakto Game|website=markhuckvale.com|access-date=2019-04-27}}</ref> at which point the player to have made the last move loses the game.<ref name=":3" /> However, in this game, unlike tic-tac-toe, there will always be a player who wins any game of Notakto.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://blogs.cornell.edu/info2040/2015/12/01/x-only-tic-tac-toe/|title=X-Only Tic Tac Toe : Networks Course blog for INFO 2040/CS 2850/Econ 2040/SOC 2090|website=blogs.cornell.edu|access-date=2016-12-18}}</ref>

Notakto is an [[impartial game]], where the allowable moves depend only on the state of the game and not on which player is taking their turn. When played across multiple boards it is a [[disjunctive sum|disjunctive game]].<ref name=":2" /> The game is attributed to professor and backgammon player [[Bob Koca]], who is said to have invented the game in 2010, when his five-year-old nephew suggested playing a game of tic-tac-toe with both players as "X".<ref name=":4"/>

== Play ==
Notakto is played on a finite number of empty three-by-three boards.<ref name=":0" /> Then, each player takes turns placing an X on the board(s) in a vacant space (a space not occupied by an X already on the board).<ref name=":1" /> If a board has a three-in-a-row, the board is dead and it cannot be played on any more.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":3">{{Cite news|url=https://www.inverse.com/article/9178-three-simple-tricks-will-make-tic-tac-toe-actually-fun-again-puzzles|title=These Three Tweaks Make Tic-Tac-Toe Not Suck|newspaper=Inverse|access-date=2016-11-25}}</ref> When one player makes a three-in-a-row and there are no more boards to play on, that player loses.<ref name=":2">{{Cite arXiv|title=The Secrets of Notakto: Winning at X-only Tic-Tac-Toe|last=Plambeck|first=Thane|last2=Whitehead|first2=Greg|date=November 24, 2016|class=math.CO|eprint=1301.1672v1}}</ref><ref name=":1" />

== Optimal strategy ==

[[File:Notakto boot trap.svg|thumb|The "finger trap", in which the first player (who started by playing the center "X") is guaranteed a win]]
The optimal strategy for a single-board game of Notakto allows the first player to force a win. It is for the first player to play the center and then play a [[Knight (chess)|knight's]] move (two squares vertically and one square horizontally, or vice versa) away from the opponent's play.<ref name=":1" /> This strategy works because it makes a boot-like structure, which is called the boot trap. From the boot trap position the first player will be able to force a win.<ref name=":1" />

With two boards, the second player should on their first move play in the center square of the empty board (the one with no Xs in it). Then, the second player sacrifices one of the boards (by making a three-in-a-row) if it is possible. Now, the game is a 1-board game of Notakto so the second player uses the knight's move or boot trap strategies to win.<ref name=":1" />

From these two strategies, any game with more than two boards can always be won by the first player (on an odd number of boards) or by the second player (on an even number of boards).<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=http://gmmentalgym.blogspot.com/2012/05/how-to-play-and-win-notakto.html|title=How to Play and Win Notakto|last=Cram|first=Scott|access-date=2016-11-26}}</ref>
